A user who uses mise and mostly likes it says it has simplified their workflow for managing environments. They don't need its task runner because Make and just already cover that, and they would prefer mise stay focused on environment management rather than growing in scope.

I'm really bullish on mise... Being able to have one config file to manage tools (node, python, rust, go, etc) as well as a simple makefile replacement makes it incredibly convenient. I always setup a postinstall hook so someone just runs `mise install` and gets correct tool versions plus dependencies installed. It's significantly more practical than nix, which has a steep learning curve.

Example from a monorepo's ansible directory: a [hooks] postinstall in mise.toml runs `uv sync` and `ansible-galaxy` role/collection installs, so after `mise install` the user also gets all needed Python packages and galaxy roles/collections.
I set up a new project with mise. It makes it so much easier for new people to get started without having to do a bunch of manual steps. Awesome tool.

Having started with Mise, and now being primarily a Nix user — Mise still has the edge for what it does. It supports pinning exact versions of many more languages than devenv does. When devenv doesn't support the version you need, it's straight back to the pain of overlays and overrides.
Mise has become almost indispensable for me within just a few months, I've rebuilt so much of our tooling around it.
I love mise so much and use it at $DAYJOB to manage a multi-service polyglot monorepo.

I was a bit slow to adopt mise because it took me a while to understand it (I came in thinking of it as a direnv replacement with more features). It especially makes life behind corporate barbed wire easier. I replaced tedious manual binary downloads from GitHub releases, and switching from pyenv to mise for Python improved the experience.
I even added some mise config lines to my global gitignore because I often use it in projects by others that don't set up mise config.

A commenter complained the mise GitHub repo has issues disabled with no explanation, saying it doesn't inspire confidence. Another user found this surprising, but said after a couple years of use they have a ton of confidence in mise and recommend it to everyone, citing its release frequency and utility.

A user who wanted task caching found that remote task caching is listed as an anti-goal on mise's roadmap; the task runner is meant to stay a simple convenience around executing scripts. Another commenter noted local caching is still very important.

I have a monorepo with mixed projects (Rust server, Svelte frontend, Terraform deployment) and shared Rust CLI tasks; mise's monorepo tasks come at just the right time to use without going insane. I had a not-so-great experience with other builders/managers, including lerna, so I love this.

I recently switched to Mise for all of my JS, ruby, python, and java sdk management needs, and I've been delighted with it so far. Not having to install RVM, NVM, some toxic brew of python installers, and SDKMan has been such a breath of fresh air.
This is nice! Jetbrains tools sometimes need a bit more configuration with it, otherwise it's very seamless.
I'm using it to unify my team's toolchain without resorting to nix or running everything in docker... the DX of mise is too good. Tasks are really nice too, all my repo scripts now have completions.

Thinking about how to use mise as a task runner in GitHub Actions: the mise repo's own workflows appear to just use a few `run: mise` steps, so you end up rewriting them and can't use task dependencies. I'd prefer a way to generate workflow files but haven't found one.
Just using mise as a drop-in asdf replacement has been delightful. Same functionality but much snappier with better UX.
Ignoring the task runner stuff, Mise is great just as a "better asdf". It allows many more package sources (including pipx, go and cargo).
Finally I can retire makefiles in my python projects.
